note.qleaf-inference-latency.qleaf.block.source: In the era of AI and deep learning, what is the point of talking about tree models? A practical reason is that they still perform well, sometimes at the state of the art, on a variety of problems involving tabular data, ranging from pattern recognition in high-energy physics to real-time decision problems in robotics. Tree models pose different challenges in training and ⟦0⟧ than neural networks do. In this note, we focus on ⟦1⟧. For example, gradient boosting, one of the most popular tree-based methods, usually produces a large number of shallow trees.

note.qleaf-inference-latency.qleaf.block.source: The large number of trees offers considerable parallelism, but their limited depth means that the processor, whether ⟦0⟧ or ⟦1⟧, does very little work per tree. This is an atypical workload for GPUs: distributing trees among threads can leave each thread with too little work to keep the ⟦2⟧ busy. In the extreme case of batch-one ⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧ and coordination can dominate end-to-end latency. These overheads are usually amortized over more computation in workloads with higher arithmetic intensity. The conventional wisdom is therefore to use a ⟦5⟧ for tree ⟦6⟧ and, when possible, parallelize the task across multiple cores.

In this note, we introduce ⟦0⟧, a systematic benchmarking framework that may also be useful in production. It exposes a common interface for multithreaded ⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧ backends. We begin with the latency ablation and the framework's structure, then examine the ⟦3⟧ implementation, with its persistent workers and lock-free handoff. We then move to a naive ⟦4⟧ implementation and work through a series of optimizations to reach a competitive ⟦5⟧ implementation. The interesting lesson is how much of the request time lies outside tree evaluation itself, and how to reduce that overhead with somewhat non-standard tricks.
⟦0⟧In this note:⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧Latency ablation⟦3⟧ · ⟦4⟧Framework⟦5⟧ · ⟦6⟧⟦7⟧⟦8⟧ · ⟦9⟧⟦10⟧⟦11⟧ · ⟦12⟧Workload dependence⟦13⟧
Start with the latency ablation

The table below traces one optimization path for ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧ depth-six ⟦2⟧ trees⟦3⟧, with ⟦4⟧ input features and ⟦5⟧ ⟦6⟧ threads per block. The persistent rows are cumulative; the one-shot row is a separate reference. Values are host-to-host latencies in microseconds.

Keeping the kernel alive initially makes the request ⟦0⟧slower⟦1⟧. Removing cross-block completion and reducing the number of request pollers produce the largest gains; changing the input handoff then brings the median below seven microseconds. We will return to the mechanism behind each row.

The timer starts before feature staging and stops when the result is available to the ⟦0⟧. For mapped input, the current feature row is copied into the mapped host buffer within that interval. Each run uses ⟦1⟧ warmup requests and ⟦2⟧ measured requests. Model loading and worker initialization are outside the steady-state measurement.

The benchmark machine has an Intel Core i7-12700F and a ⟦0⟧ GiB ⟦1⟧-capable consumer ⟦2⟧. ⟦3⟧ turbo is disabled in the main comparisons; ⟦4⟧ application clocks are requested at ⟦5⟧ MHz for the SMs and ⟦6⟧ MHz for memory. The second workload, ⟦7⟧, has ⟦8⟧ features instead of ⟦9⟧. Both use depth-six ensembles of ⟦10⟧, ⟦11⟧, ⟦12⟧, and ⟦13⟧ trees. The ⟦14⟧full benchmark⟦15⟧ records the distributions, configurations, and data provenance.
The framework: model, workers, and reduction

The central interface is ⟦0⟧. It owns the model representation, partitions the forest among workers, submits a feature row, and collects the workers' results. The current prediction output is a scalar raw margin: the sum of the tree outputs.

⟦0⟧ types select the node layout, worker implementation, load balancer, and reducer. Runtime JSON supplies the model and worker settings, such as ⟦1⟧ affinity. This makes it possible to change the execution policy while retaining the same prediction interface and workload.
The forest and workers are prepared once. Prediction reuses them for each input row.
⟦0⟧Node buffer:⟦1⟧ stores the tree data. ⟦2⟧ keeps split values and feature indices in separate arrays; ⟦3⟧ provides a direct node layout.
⟦0⟧Load balancer:⟦1⟧ assigns groups of trees to workers. The default ⟦2⟧ divides the tree count evenly.
⟦0⟧Worker:⟦1⟧ evaluates its assigned trees. ⟦2⟧ traversal, ⟦3⟧ bitmask evaluation, and ⟦4⟧ workers fit the same interface. ⟦5⟧ adds a persistent host thread around a ⟦6⟧ worker.
⟦0⟧Reducer:⟦1⟧ combines the workers' partial sums. ⟦2⟧ adds them to produce the margin.
At the interface level, a request is simply:

Internally, the inferrer submits the row to all workers before collecting their results, allowing threaded workers to evaluate their partitions concurrently. A ⟦0⟧ worker manages its own grid of blocks: another level of parallelism inside the worker.
The implementation is in ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧⟦2⟧, with ⟦3⟧ policies and workers in ⟦4⟧⟦5⟧⟦6⟧.
⟦0⟧: do little work per tree and keep workers ready
Follow one path through each tree

For a depth-six binary tree, ⟦0⟧ needs six split decisions followed by a leaf value. It does not need to inspect every internal node. ⟦1⟧'s branch-traversal worker computes the next node index arithmetically at each depth and accumulates leaf values across its trees.

This is a small loop over a compact model representation. The code exposes the absence of aliasing to the compiler, leaving room for vectorization across trees. The dependency within a single path remains: the next feature and threshold depend on the preceding comparison.

The alternative bitmask worker evaluates conditions and intersects masks of reachable leaves. That creates more regular work, but also requires more comparisons than following one path. For shallow trees, the extra work must earn its place through parallel execution.
Create threads once, then hand off requests

Launching and joining threads around every prediction would add setup and scheduling work to a request lasting only a few microseconds. ⟦0⟧ instead constructs persistent threads with the inferrer. Each thread owns a tree partition and can be pinned to a ⟦1⟧ core.
The upper row illustrates per-request thread creation; it is not a separately measured benchmark baseline. ⟦0⟧ keeps its workers alive between requests.

The handoff uses atomics rather than a mutex-protected task queue. The caller publishes the feature pointer with a release store. The worker observes it with an acquire load, evaluates its partition, and publishes a ready flag with release semantics. The caller waits with an acquire load before reading the result. The feature row remains valid until prediction completes.

The pointer and ready flag form a small request/response protocol, with one request in flight. This avoids a thread launch or blocking wakeup on the steady-state path. Workers spin while waiting, so this low-latency configuration occupies cores even between requests.
Thread placement is part of the algorithm

On a hybrid ⟦0⟧, “eight threads” is not a complete configuration. Physical cores, SMT siblings, and efficiency cores are not interchangeable. The benchmark compares physical-first placement with sibling-first placement, reserving a logical ⟦1⟧ for dispatch.

Physical-first placement wins ⟦0⟧ of ⟦1⟧ comparisons with two, four, or eight workers. At ⟦2⟧ workers, sibling-first wins seven of eight comparisons. The latter ordering can use the performance cores' SMT siblings before spilling work onto efficiency cores.

For ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧ trees, eight workers take ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧ µs⟦4⟧ with physical-first placement and ⟦5⟧⟦6⟧ µs⟦7⟧ with sibling-first placement. At ⟦8⟧ workers, the ordering reverses: ⟦9⟧⟦10⟧ µs⟦11⟧ versus ⟦12⟧⟦13⟧ µs⟦14⟧. More workers help only if the work distribution and placement justify the additional coordination.

These ⟦0⟧ results use the no-turbo policy. The separate turbo-enabled ⟦1⟧ reference reaches ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧ µs⟦4⟧ for ⟦5⟧ ⟦6⟧ trees and ⟦7⟧⟦8⟧ µs⟦9⟧ for ⟦10⟧ ⟦11⟧ trees. A host-only request avoids the device round trip entirely, and ⟦12⟧ frequency matters at this timescale.
⟦0⟧: spend the latency budget on tree evaluation
⟦0⟧. A kernel launch for every request

The simplest ⟦0⟧ path launches a grid, evaluates the forest, waits for completion, and returns block partials to the host for the final sum. The forest is already on the ⟦1⟧; it is not transferred afresh for each prediction.

A thread can follow one tree path while many trees are processed in parallel. There is little arithmetic per tree, so kernel launch, input movement, synchronization, and result visibility account for significant parts of the request time. More arithmetic throughput does not remove those costs.
The measurement includes both crossings and completion. This is a data-flow diagram, not a measured breakdown of time.
⟦0⟧. Keep the kernel resident

A persistent kernel is launched once and loops over requests. This is the ⟦0⟧ counterpart of the ⟦1⟧ worker pool: setup is moved out of the steady-state path, and each new row arrives through a handoff protocol.
Persistence removes repeated launches. The kernel still needs to detect requests and make results visible to the host.

The initial persistent implementation copies the feature row into device memory, advances a sequence flag, lets every block poll it, and combines block results through device-wide completion logic. Its ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧ µs⟦2⟧ median exceeds the one-shot mapped-input reference's ⟦3⟧⟦4⟧ µs⟦5⟧. The comparison changes the input path as well as the launch policy; it demonstrates the cost of the initial design rather than isolating launch overhead.

When the protocol requires all blocks to make progress, the persistent grid must fit on the device. ⟦0⟧ checks co-residency instead of assuming an arbitrarily large grid can participate in the handshake.
⟦0⟧. Let blocks finish independently; reduce on the host

Each block first reduces its own tree outputs locally. The initial design atomically adds that partial sum to a shared device result and updates a shared completion counter. The last arriving block publishes the completed result and signals the host.
The blocks evaluate trees independently but contend on shared state when finishing. Atomic accumulation and final-arriver coordination introduce a serial step into the request.

The alternative retains local block reduction and removes the shared completion step. ⟦0⟧Each block writes its sum into its own host-visible, pinned result slot.⟦1⟧ The ⟦2⟧ waits until all slots have been filled, then sums the values in the small array of block results.
Moving the final reduction to the host removes the ⟦0⟧'s shared completion point. Each block still reduces its own tree results.
For ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧ trees, the median falls from ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧ to ⟦4⟧ µs⟦5⟧, and p99 from ⟦6⟧⟦7⟧ to ⟦8⟧ µs⟦9⟧. A little extra work on the ⟦10⟧ simplifies the device path.

An unfilled slot contains NaN; a non-NaN partial sum also serves as its completion marker. The host collects the results and rearms the slots. This relies on non-NaN partial sums and the single-request protocol. Independent slots remove contention between blocks, while publication and buffer reuse still require a well-defined protocol.
⟦0⟧. One block polls the host; the others wait on device state
A system-visible request flag is expensive when every block repeatedly reads it. Many consumers inspecting the same flag generate traffic without doing useful tree work.

The single-poller policy assigns this job to block zero, which detects a request and updates a device-scope broadcast sequence. Other blocks wait on that device-side sequence. In the staged variants, block zero also prepares the feature row before broadcasting readiness.

This changes ⟦0⟧where⟦1⟧ the waiting occurs: most blocks no longer observe host-visible request state. For ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧ trees, the median falls from ⟦4⟧⟦5⟧ to ⟦6⟧ µs⟦7⟧. For ⟦8⟧ trees, it instead rises slightly, from ⟦9⟧⟦10⟧ to ⟦11⟧ µs⟦12⟧. With fewer blocks, the additional broadcast stage has less traffic to eliminate.
⟦0⟧. Mapped pinned input versus an explicit copy

Pinned memory is host memory whose pages are kept resident. It can serve as a source for explicit transfers. Mapping additionally makes it accessible to ⟦0⟧ loads and stores. On a discrete ⟦1⟧, mapped host access still crosses the interconnect: “zero copy” avoids an explicit copy into a separate device buffer, not physical data movement. ⟦2⟧NVIDIA's memory guide⟦3⟧ explains the distinction.
Pinning and copying are separate choices. Mapping removes a per-request copy operation; staging can keep repeated feature reads on the ⟦0⟧.

For a small row, issuing and completing a copy can cost more than moving its bytes. ⟦0⟧ has only ⟦1⟧⟦2⟧ bytes⟦3⟧ of float features. After the poll storm has been removed, mapped input reduces the ⟦4⟧-tree median from ⟦5⟧⟦6⟧ to ⟦7⟧ µs⟦8⟧.

Direct access is less attractive if many workers repeatedly fetch a large row from host memory. Staging addresses that reuse problem: the leader reads the row into a device buffer, publishes readiness, and workers evaluate against that staged copy. The ⟦0⟧ still writes each row into the mapped input buffer; this host-side copy remains inside the benchmark's timing interval.
⟦0⟧. Let the data signal its own arrival
The sequence-flag protocol separates data publication from notification: prepare the features, then publish an ordered request flag. The sentinel protocol folds those operations together.

Before a request, the mapped input contains reserved sentinel values. The ⟦0⟧ writes the row. The leader checks and stages features until every value has arrived, resets the mapped input to sentinels, and broadcasts the request through device-side state. Evaluation reads the staged row, so resetting the input does not destroy the data being processed.

The host waits for all results before sending another row. Feature values must be finite and must not use the reserved ⟦0⟧ sentinels. Under this protocol, data arrival replaces a separate host-visible request flag in the steady-state handoff.

For ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧ trees, the median falls from ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧ to ⟦4⟧ µs⟦5⟧ and p99 from ⟦6⟧⟦7⟧ to ⟦8⟧ µs⟦9⟧. The gain is smaller than those from the earlier coordination changes. This ablation switches staging and sentinel signaling together, so it does not measure either change in isolation.
⟦0⟧. Expose useful parallelism within each tree

Traversal follows only one path, but successive steps depend on earlier comparisons. Bitmask evaluation performs more comparisons and combines masks of possible leaves. Its potential advantage is that several lanes can share that work.

At one thread per tree, the extra work generally loses: the staged persistent bitmask path takes ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧ µs⟦2⟧ for ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧ trees. Tuning to four threads per tree reduces it to ⟦5⟧⟦6⟧ µs⟦7⟧, still above traversal's ⟦8⟧⟦9⟧ µs⟦10⟧ in the controlled comparison.

Layout also matters. Node-major storage places the same node position from neighboring trees together, which can improve coalescing when neighboring lanes process different trees. When several lanes process one tree, another layout may be preferable. For ⟦0⟧, tuned bitmask workers with a row-major layout are the best ⟦1⟧ variants at ⟦2⟧ and ⟦3⟧ trees. Layout and threads per tree need to be considered together.
⟦0⟧. Cache trees where the resident working set fits

A persistent kernel can retain tree data in shared memory across requests, avoiding repeated reads of those nodes from global memory. This benefit comes at the cost of a larger shared-memory footprint, which can limit the number of resident blocks.

For ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧ trees, the matched uncached traversal in the cache sweep takes ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧ µs⟦4⟧, compared with ⟦5⟧⟦6⟧ µs⟦7⟧ for one-wave caching. The best uncached result from the broader sweep is ⟦8⟧⟦9⟧ µs⟦10⟧; using the matched comparison separates caching from block-size tuning. The ⟦11⟧-tree cached persistent variants are skipped because their grids are not co-resident.
What changes with the workload?

The ⟦0⟧ feature row is about ⟦1⟧⟦2⟧ KiB⟦3⟧, rather than ⟦4⟧'s ⟦5⟧ bytes. At ⟦6⟧ trees, removing cross-block completion and choosing a polling policy reduces ⟦7⟧ traversal from ⟦8⟧⟦9⟧ to ⟦10⟧ µs⟦11⟧. Adding mapped/staged signaling increases it to ⟦12⟧⟦13⟧ µs⟦14⟧. The copied-input path is preferable here.

This helps explain why ⟦0⟧ exposes policies instead of choosing one configuration for every workload. Feature width changes communication cost. Forest size changes the work available to distribute. Tree depth and evaluation method change the work within each tree. Shared-memory use changes which persistent grids can remain resident.

For batch-one ⟦0⟧, optimization starts with a good ⟦1⟧ implementation and a measurement of the complete request. On the ⟦2⟧, removing repeated launches is only the first step. Reducing the overhead of cross-block completion, host polling, and input handoff is what makes the persistent path competitive. The resulting latency is increasingly shaped by communication and result visibility; the ablation shows how to reduce those costs without itself measuring a physical communication lower bound.
The ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧ repository⟦2⟧ contains the framework. The ⟦3⟧benchmark report used here⟦4⟧ and ⟦5⟧source at the same revision⟦6⟧ provide the full configurations and implementation details.

project.NESSi 2.0.description.source: A shared research library for nonequilibrium Green’s functions and interacting quantum systems. Version ⟦0⟧ adds memory-truncated time propagation and steady-state calculations.

project.NESSi 2.0.detail.source: I contributed to the development of ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧ through my research on nonequilibrium many-body methods. The package supports accurate numerical integration and distributed-memory calculations for quantum dynamics.

project.OptIndex.description.source: A safe intrusive object store with stable addresses and compile-time index definitions. Centralized storage and object lifetime management keep optional or partitioned views consistent without duplicating objects.

project.OptIndex.detail.source: Built for bounded working sets and repeated queries, with explicit indexing control and an optional fixed-size pool. The design addresses consistency across indices without duplicating the stored objects.

project.QLeaf.detail.source: ⟦0⟧ aggressively optimizes data transfer and cross-block coordination, and uses a lock-free ⟦1⟧ to bring end-to-end latency close to the limits of host–device communication.

project.QuDrip.description.source: A toolbox for constructing constrained Hilbert spaces, quantum operators, and Hamiltonians. Sparse-matrix and Krylov methods support ground-state calculations, real-time evolution, and Lindblad dynamics.
